summary: Describes 464XLAT, an architecture giving limited IPv4 connectivity across an IPv6-only network by combining stateless translation at the edge, as in RFC 6145, with stateful translation in the core, as in RFC 6146. It helps deploy IPv4 service quickly. It is informational.

eli5.summary: An old-language letter is translated into the new language at your door, and translated again at the big post office, so you can talk to old-language friends.

questions: how do ipv4 apps work on ipv6 only networks
what is the difference between clat and plat
subtitle: How IPv4-only apps keep working on an IPv6-only network by translating twice.

tldr.problem: As unallocated IPv4 address pools run out, many networks will struggle to give end users IPv4 addresses, yet some applications still need IPv4.
tldr.mechanism: A customer-side translator (CLAT) does stateless translation at the edge and a provider-side translator (PLAT) does stateful translation in the core, so IPv4 traffic crosses an IPv6-only network without encapsulation.
tldr.outcome: It gives limited IPv4 service (client to server only) over IPv6-only access networks using existing translation standards, without new protocols.

facts.label: CLAT prefixes to acquire
facts.value: A /64 each for uplink, downlinks and translation

today: RFC 6877 is an Informational document and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the translation standards RFC 6145 and RFC 6146.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
With IPv4 address pools exhausted, it will be hard for many networks to assign IPv4 addresses to end users. 464XLAT is an IPv4-over-IPv6 technique that extends IPv4 service across an IPv6-only network while encouraging IPv6 deployment.

It is not a full replacement for IPv4. It supports IPv4 only in the client-server model, where the server has a global IPv4 address, so it does not suit IPv4 peer-to-peer communication or inbound IPv4 connections. Native IPv6 keeps full any-to-any communication.

The design reuses the translation standards RFC 6145 (stateless) and RFC 6146 (stateful). It does not require DNS64 (RFC 6147), because an IPv4 host can simply send IPv4 packets, even to an IPv4 DNS server, and they are translated on the way.
sections.eli5: Some old apps only speak the old address language. This trick lets them keep talking even though the road in between only understands the new language.

sections.title: CLAT and PLAT
sections.content:
Two translators do the work. The CLAT (customer-side translator) complies with RFC 6145 and algorithmically translates 1:1 between private IPv4 addresses and global IPv6 addresses. It can live in a router or in an end node such as a mobile phone. The PLAT (provider-side translator) complies with RFC 6146 and translates N:1 between global IPv6 addresses and global IPv4 addresses.

In the wireline topology, private IPv4 hosts behind the CLAT reach global IPv4 hosts through translation at both the CLAT and the PLAT, while IPv6 hosts reach IPv6 hosts directly without translation. In the 3GPP wireless topology, the CLAT on the user equipment gives applications a private IPv4 address and an IPv4 default route, and the mobile network provides the PLAT.
sections.eli5: One translator sits in your home and one sits at the provider. Your letter is translated once leaving home and again before reaching an old-language server.

sections.title: How Traffic Is Treated
sections.content:
What happens depends on the server and the application. If both are IPv6, traffic is end-to-end IPv6 with no translation. If the server is IPv4 and the application is IPv6, the PLAT does stateful translation. If both are IPv4, traffic gets 464XLAT double translation at the PLAT and CLAT.

The double translation is stateless when a dedicated /64 is available for translation on the CLAT. Otherwise the CLAT performs NAT44 from the LAN to a single IPv4 address and then translates statelessly to a single IPv6 address, so it has both stateful and stateless parts.

On a 3GPP network, the CLAT is used only when needed, for example for IPv4 literals or IPv4-only sockets.
sections.eli5: If both ends speak the new language, no translator is needed. If an old-language app talks to an old-language server, both translators step in.

sections.title: Implementation Notes for the CLAT
sections.content:
The IPv6 address format follows Section 2.2 of RFC 6052. The CLAT should acquire a /64 for the uplink interface, a /64 for all downlink interfaces and a dedicated /64 for statelessly translated packets, for example through DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation. It must also discover the PLAT-side translation prefix, which it uses as the destination for traffic needing stateful translation.

The CLAT should implement a DNS proxy as in RFC 5625 and set itself as the DNS server via DHCP or other means. This avoids sending IPv4 DNS lookups through both translations, so only IPv6 native queries cross the access network. DNS queries not sent to the proxy must still be allowed and are translated like any other traffic.

A router with a CLAT should also provide ordinary router services such as DHCP of private addresses, DHCPv6, Router Advertisement and DNS service. For peer-to-peer use, ICE may be used, since 464XLAT is a hub and spoke design.
sections.eli5: The home translator should also act as a helpful receptionist for names and addresses, so the long trip does not have to be translated more than needed.

sections.title: Deployment and Security
sections.content:
The RFC lists several motivations: minimal IPv4 resource needs through statistical multiplexing, no new protocols, IPv6-only networks that are simpler and cheaper than dual-stack ones, and native IP monitoring and traffic engineering without the indirection of a tunnel. An ISP can do traffic engineering by IPv4 destination even when another ISP runs the PLAT, because the IPv4 destination can be read from the translated IPv6 header.

For security, the RFC points to Section 5 of RFC 6146 for implementing a PLAT and Section 7 of RFC 6145 for a CLAT, and notes that a CLAT may comply with RFC 6092.
sections.eli5: Because the translated letters still carry readable addresses, the post office can sort and watch them easily, which a sealed package would not allow.
